title: Pork and vegetables (no carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens, potatoes, sauce)

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of lean pork sautéed with a mix of vegetables, deliberately excluding carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens and potatoes. No sauce is added, allowing the natural juices of the meat and vegetables to shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork provides high‑quality protein and vitamin B12.
Excluding carrots and broccoli reduces beta‑carotene content while retaining other phytochemicals from the remaining vegetables.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables are often left out in low‑oxalate diets.
A sauce‑free preparation is suitable for those avoiding added sugar and excess sodium.
When cooked properly, pork stays juicy and flavorful even without additional sauces.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Pork supplies all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6) support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish provides iron, zinc and selenium, important for immune health and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Low carbohydrate content
items.content: Omitting potatoes and sauce makes the meal suitable for low‑carb eating patterns.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: Remaining vegetables such as bell pepper, zucchini and cauliflower add dietary fiber for digestive health.

items.title: Food allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to pork or specific vegetables used.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salt is added, monitor the amount to stay within recommended daily limits.

items.title: Cooking safety
items.content: Undercooked pork can harbor harmful bacteria; ensure an internal temperature of 71 °C (160 °F).

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: If high‑oxalate vegetables (e.g., spinach) are included, people prone to kidney stones should limit them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main course, optionally alongside whole‑grain sides such as quinoa or brown rice. Vegetables can be eaten whole, sliced, or mashed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat thoroughly before serving.
